summary: Defines a set of RADIUS attributes to support compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks, such as which tunnel type and where it ends. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: These are the extra fields a central server can send saying which private pipe to put a new connection into and where it leads.

what is tunnel type 3 in radius
subtitle: RADIUS attributes that tell a network access server which tunnel to build, where, and how to authenticate it.

tldr.problem: In dial-up networks, a tunnel is sometimes created for the user without their choice (compulsory tunneling), so the RADIUS server needs a way to hand tunnel details to the tunnel endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines ten RADIUS attributes (Tunnel-Type, Tunnel-Medium-Type, endpoints, password, group, assignment, preference and authentication names), grouped by a one-octet Tag so several alternative tunnels can be described in one packet.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2865 and is itself updated by RFC 3575. The attributes carry tunnel data but offer no end-to-end protection for users.

today: RFC 2868 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2865, and it is itself updated by RFC 3575. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Attributes Are Needed
sections.content:
Many uses of tunneling protocols such as L2TP involve dial-up network access. Some are voluntary tunneling, where the tunnel is created at the user's request. Others are compulsory tunneling: the tunnel is created without any action from the user and without allowing the user any choice.

To provide compulsory tunneling, new RADIUS attributes are needed to carry tunneling information from the RADIUS server to the tunnel end points. RFC 2868 defines them. Specific recommendations and examples for L2TP are in RFC 2809. The memo updates RFC 2865, and its accounting counterpart is RFC 2867.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the network sends your traffic through a private pipe without asking you. The gatekeeper server needs a standard way to tell the equipment at both ends of the pipe how to set it up.

sections.title: Tags and Multiple Tunnels
sections.content:
A single RADIUS packet can hold several instances of each attribute. Attributes that apply to the same tunnel SHOULD all carry the same value in their Tag field; otherwise the Tag SHOULD NOT be used. Valid tag values are 0x01 through 0x1F, and an unused tag field MUST be zero for the fixed-size attributes.

If the server returns attributes for several tunnels, the tunnel initiator SHOULD treat them as alternatives. The server SHOULD include a Tunnel-Preference attribute in each set, and the numerically lowest value is the most preferred, from 0x000000 (most preferred) to 0xFFFFFF (least). If preferences are equal, the initiator uses local metrics.

For the string attributes, a Tag above 0x1F is not a tag at all: it SHOULD be read as the first byte of the string.
sections.eli5: If the gatekeeper hands you notes for two different pipes, it puts the same sticker number on all notes for the same pipe, and a ranking so you know which pipe to try first.

sections.title: The Ten Tunnel Attributes
sections.content:
Each attribute is a standard RADIUS Type, Length, Tag, then value or string. In summary:

  • Tunnel-Type (64): which tunneling protocol, for example PPTP, L2F, L2TP, GRE or ESP. A tunnel initiator that receives only unknown or unsupported types MUST behave as though an Access-Reject had been received.
  • Tunnel-Medium-Type (65): the transport medium, using the Address Family Numbers (1 is IPv4, 2 is IPv6).
  • Tunnel-Client-Endpoint (66) and Tunnel-Server-Endpoint (67): the addresses of the initiator and server ends. For IPv4 and IPv6 it is a dotted-decimal or text address or an FQDN; implementations MUST support dotted-decimal for IPv4. Together with Acct-Tunnel-Connection-ID they can identify a tunnel globally for accounting.
  • Tunnel-Password (69): a password to authenticate to a remote server. It may only be included in an Access-Accept packet.
  • Tunnel-Private-Group-ID (81): the group ID for a tunneled session, with no restriction on its format.
  • Tunnel-Assignment-ID (82): tells the initiator which tunnel a session belongs to, so sessions can share a multiplexed tunnel or get their own.
  • Tunnel-Preference (83): ranks alternative tunnels.
  • Tunnel-Client-Auth-ID (90) and Tunnel-Server-Auth-ID (91): the names used by the initiator and the terminator during tunnel authentication, SHOULD be in UTF-8.

For Tunnel-Assignment-ID, an existing tunnel with that ID between the same endpoints is reused; otherwise a new one is established. Sessions without the attribute go to an unnamed tunnel, and the initiator MUST NOT put such a session in a named tunnel.
sections.eli5: Each attribute is one note: which kind of pipe, which road it travels, where it starts and ends, the secret word, a team label, a ranking, and the names both ends use to prove who they are.

sections.title: Hiding the Tunnel Password
sections.content:
The Tunnel-Password attribute carries a Salt field of two octets, whose most significant bit MUST be set, and whose value MUST be unique within each Access-Accept packet. Its String field holds a one-octet Data-Length, the password and optional padding of 1 to 15 octets so the total is a multiple of 16.

The String is encrypted in 16-octet blocks with MD5. The first block uses b(1) = MD5(S + R + A), where S is the shared secret, R is the 128-bit Request Authenticator from the Access-Request and A is the salt. Each ciphertext block is the plaintext block XOR b(i), and later keys are b(i) = MD5(S + c(i-1)). The receiver reverses the process.
sections.eli5: The secret word is scrambled with a key made from a shared secret and a one-time number, so a wandering eavesdropper sees gibberish instead of the word.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method used to hide the Tunnel-Password lets intervening RADIUS proxies learn its contents. So it SHOULD NOT be included in Access-Accept packets that may pass through relatively untrusted proxies. It also SHOULD NOT be returned to an unauthenticated client: if the Access-Request lacked a verified Signature Attribute (from RFC 2869), the Access-Accept SHOULD NOT contain the attribute.

Tunnel protocols offer security from none (for example PPTP) to strong (for example IPSec). In compulsory tunneling, any such protection applies only between the tunnel endpoints, so end users SHOULD NOT rely on it and tunnel encryption MUST NOT be treated as a replacement for end-to-end security.
sections.eli5: The secret word is hidden from outsiders but not from the helpers in the middle, and the pipe only protects the stretch between its two ends, so keep your own lock on important things.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The memo defines two lists of numbers for IANA to maintain. Tunnel-Type values 1 to 12 and Tunnel-Medium-Type values 1 to 15 are defined by this document. The remaining values in each list are available for assignment by IANA with IETF Consensus.
sections.eli5: A librarian keeps the official list of numbers. The first few are already taken, and new ones are given out only after the community agrees.
